rich_summary: This section explains the Sankhya distinction between Prakriti (material nature) and Purusha (pure consciousness). Through a series of analogies—reed and sheath, worm and fruit, fish and water, fire and pot, lotus leaf and water—the text emphasizes that two things may coexist intimately yet remain fundamentally separate. Misunderstanding this relationship leads to spiritual ignorance. Yajnavalkya then turns to Yoga, declaring that Sankhya and Yoga ultimately pursue the same goal: liberation. Yoga works through discipline of breath and senses, progressing from concentration with attributes to a higher state beyond distinctions. By withdrawing the senses and fixing the mind step by step toward the Supreme, the yogin reaches samadhi—an unmoving, lamp‑like stillness in which the radiant Brahman is realized, leading eventually to emancipation.

highlight_spans.why: Key philosophical claim: Prakriti appears stable though it is inherently unstable.
Captures the paradox of appearance versus reality central to Sankhya metaphysics.
Introduces Prakriti, one of the two fundamental principles contrasted throughout the passage.

top_scenes.scene_text: A serene yogi in deep samadhi sits motionless like a steady lamp flame burning in a windless dark cave.
A lotus leaf floating on still water with droplets rolling off it, symbolizing detachment between Purusha and Prakriti.
A calm ascetic carefully climbing steps while holding a brimming vessel of oil as armed men threaten him, yet not a drop spills.
